appraisal_events.evidence: Il la reconnaît comme une prostituée qu'il a connue trivialement, "une femme quelconque qui pour vingt francs ferait tout ce que je voudrais"; mais il ajoute ensuite "Ce n'était pas «Rachel quand du Seigneur» qui me semblait peu de chose, c'était la puissance de l'imagination humaine... que je trouvais grandes."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator recalls Rachel as an ordinary, mercenary woman known through a trivial commercial encounter, sharply undercutting Saint-Loup's exalted image of her; but the narrator explicitly redirects the smallness away from her onto the illusion-making power of imagination, so the diminishment is qualified rather than flatly endorsed.

appraisal_events.evidence: "il donnait plus d'un million pour avoir... ce qui m'avait été offert comme à chacun pour vingt francs"; l'inquiétude, le tourment, l'amour de Saint-Loup ont fait de ce qui était pour le narrateur "un jouet mécanique" "un objet de souffrances infinies, le prix même de l'existence."
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup is portrayed as emotionally captive to an illusion he cannot see through or escape, paying enormously in suffering and money for what the narrator knows firsthand to be materially trivial, a sympathetic but still diminishing picture of dependency and blindness.

status_effects.explanation: Her local standing in the narrator's account is lowered by being recalled as a trivial, mercenary prostitute, though the narrator's own closing reversal partially retracts this judgment.

Saint-Loup is shown as dependent on and captive to an illusion, suffering and paying vastly disproportionate emotional and material cost for what is, in the narrator's flat knowledge, ordinary and cheap.

ambiguities: The narrator explicitly reverses a straightforward reading of Rachel's diminishment near the end of the passage ('Ce n'était pas «Rachel quand du Seigneur» qui me semblait peu de chose, c'était la puissance de l'imagination humaine... que je trouvais grandes'), redirecting the evaluative weight from Rachel herself to the illusion-generating power of imagination; this materially softens how E1 should be read.
